title: St. Patrick's Day Hangover: How to Drink Smart and Recover Fast
excerpt: Why St. Patrick's Day hangovers hit so hard, whether green beer or day drinking makes it worse, how many drinks a pint of Guinness really is, and a simple plan for the day and the morning after.
metaDescription: Why St. Patrick's Day hangovers hit so hard, whether green beer and day drinking make it worse, and a simple plan to pace the day and recover on March 18.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** St. Patrick's Day hangovers are usually worse than a normal night out for one simple reason: the day is long. Parades start in the morning, pubs fill up by lunch, and many people are still going at midnight. That can mean ten or twelve hours of drinking, often with little real food, plenty of carbonated beer, a few rounds of Irish whiskey, and a late, short night of sleep. Green beer, Guinness, and day drinking get the blame, but the size of the hangover mostly comes down to how much you drink in total and how fast. The good news is that a few decisions made before you leave the house can make March 18 a lot easier.

**The quick plan:** Eat a real breakfast with protein and fat. Pick your ride home before your first drink. Aim for no more than about one standard drink per hour, with a glass of water between rounds. Eat again around lunch and again in the evening. Skip the chugged shots and the dropped-shot drinks. Drink water and get to bed rather than "rallying" for a second wind. In the morning, rehydrate, eat, and if you need a painkiller, take ibuprofen with food rather than reaching for acetaminophen after a very heavy day.

> **Get home safe. Decide it now.** Before you leave, settle exactly how you're getting home: a sober friend who has agreed to drive, a rideshare app with your payment card already set up, public transit you know runs late, or a couch at a friend's place. US traffic-safety agencies run drunk-driving campaigns around St. Patrick's Day every year because the holiday brings long drinking days and lots of people on the road. Day drinking makes this trickier, because you may feel "fine" by early evening after drinking since noon. You're not. And if you drank heavily late into the night, you may still be over the legal limit the next morning.

> **When to get help right away.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone** can't be woken up, is breathing very slowly or irregularly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute, or pauses of 10 seconds or more), has a seizure, is vomiting while passed out or confused, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and it can kill. Don't leave the person to "sleep it off." Roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit, stay with them, and get help. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to look for.

## Why St. Patrick's Day Drinking Hits Harder Than a Normal Night

A hangover isn't caused by one thing. Researchers think it comes from several effects stacking up: acetaldehyde (the toxic chemical your liver makes when it starts breaking down alcohol), an immune and inflammation response, poor-quality sleep, low blood sugar, stomach irritation, and fluid loss. St. Patrick's Day manages to push on nearly all of them at once.

- **The hours are long.** Most nights out run three to five hours. St. Patrick's Day can easily run from a late-morning parade to closing time. Even a "moderate" pace adds up to a big total when the clock runs that long.
- **The drinks are big.** A pint is not one drink. A US pint of regular beer is about one and a third standard drinks, and an imperial pint (the 20-ounce glass some Irish pubs use) is closer to one and a half or more, depending on the beer. People who count pints as drinks undercount by a lot.
- **Food gets skipped.** It's easy to grab a pastry before the parade and then not eat a proper meal until the evening, if at all. Drinking on an empty stomach makes your blood alcohol rise faster and higher.
- **Shots and novelty drinks speed things up.** Irish whiskey rounds and dropped-shot drinks are designed to be drunk fast. Fast drinking is what pushes blood alcohol up sharply and causes the memory gaps people call blackouts.
- **Sleep takes a hit.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it disrupts the second half of the night, so you wake up early and unrested. If you crash in the early evening and then wake at 2 a.m., you get the worst of both worlds.
- **It's often cold.** Mid-March can be chilly in much of the US and Europe. Standing outside at a parade while drinking makes you feel warmer than you are, because alcohol widens blood vessels near the skin. That actually lets your body lose heat faster.

None of this is unique to March 17. It's just that this one day tends to combine all of them.

## Day Drinking on St. Patrick's Day: Is It Worse?

There is no good evidence that alcohol consumed in daylight causes a worse hangover, drink for drink, than the same alcohol at night. Your liver doesn't care what time it is. What makes day drinking rough is what usually comes with it:

1. **More total alcohol.** Starting at 11 a.m. instead of 8 p.m. gives you many more hours to drink. That's the main driver.
2. **Less food.** Day drinking often replaces lunch rather than following it.
3. **Sun, warmth, or cold, plus less water.** Outdoor events make it easy to forget plain water entirely.
4. **The "second wind" trap.** Many day drinkers feel tired and sluggish by late afternoon as the first drinks wear off. Instead of calling it, they have another drink or an energy drink to push through, which adds alcohol and keeps them up later.
5. **A messed-up sleep schedule.** An early-evening nap followed by more drinking, or a 7 p.m. crash followed by a 3 a.m. wake-up, leaves you short on the deep, restful sleep that helps you recover.

### How to day drink smarter

- **Start later than the most eager people in your group.** If the plan is a breakfast pub, have coffee and food there and start the beer an hour or two in. You'll still be part of the day.
- **Build in a real break.** A one- to two-hour stretch mid-afternoon where you eat, drink water, and maybe switch to a non-alcoholic beer lets your body catch up. Many pubs now carry a decent alcohol-free stout or lager.
- **Set an end time, not just a drink count.** "I'm heading home by 9" is easier to stick to after a few pints than "I'll stop at six drinks."
- **Avoid using energy drinks to keep going.** Caffeine can make you feel less drunk than you are, which tends to lead to more drinking, and it adds to the poor sleep later.

## Does Green Beer Give You a Worse Hangover?

No. There's no good evidence that green beer causes a worse hangover than the same beer without the color. Green beer is almost always an ordinary light lager with a few drops of food coloring added, either at the bar or at the brewery. The amount of dye in a glass is tiny, and food dyes aren't known to cause hangover symptoms.

What green beer does tend to have going against it:

- **It's usually cheap, light lager served in big volumes.** It goes down easily, so people drink a lot of it quickly. The hangover comes from the volume, not the color.
- **It's often served in pitchers or as party specials.** That makes it hard to track how much you've actually had.

### Why your poop might be green the next day

If you had a lot of green beer, don't be surprised to see green or dark green stool the next day. Some of the food coloring passes through your gut without being absorbed. This is harmless and should clear up within a day or two. If you see green stool along with severe diarrhea, belly pain, or fever, or if it keeps going for several days, that's a different story and worth a call to a doctor. Black, tarry stool or red blood is never something to blame on green beer and should be checked promptly.

## Guinness, Irish Whiskey, and Dropped-Shot Drinks: What Hits Hardest?

St. Patrick's Day has its own drink menu, and the choices make a difference.

### Guinness and other stouts

Guinness Draught is a fairly low-alcohol beer, around 4.2% ABV, which is lower than many American lagers and well below most craft IPAs. Despite its heavy look, a pint of it doesn't carry more alcohol than a pint of light lager. Darker beers do contain more congeners, the by-products of fermentation that give drinks their color and flavor, and some research suggests congeners can make hangovers a bit worse. A well-known study by Rohsenow and colleagues, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010, found that people rated hangovers as somewhat worse after bourbon than after the same amount of vodka. The effect of congeners is real but smaller than the effect of how much you drink. A few pints of stout won't wreck you on their own. Ten will. For more on beer in particular, see our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover).

### Irish whiskey

A standard shot of Irish whiskey (1.5 ounces at 40% ABV) is one standard drink, the same as a regular beer. The problem isn't the whiskey itself. It's that shots are fast and often come in rounds, so one round turns into three, and those land on top of the pints. Whiskey is also a darker spirit with more congeners than vodka or gin. If you like whiskey, sip one neat or with water instead of shooting it. Our [whiskey hangover guide](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) goes deeper.

### Irish coffee

Irish coffee pairs a shot of whiskey with coffee, sugar, and cream. It's one standard drink, but the caffeine can make you feel more alert than you really are. It's fine as a single treat, especially at a cold outdoor parade. It's not a way to "sober up."

### Dropped-shot drinks

The drink known in the US as an "Irish car bomb" is a shot of Irish cream and Irish whiskey dropped into a half pint of stout and chugged before the cream curdles. Many Irish people find the name offensive, given its reference to bombings during the Troubles, and bartenders in Ireland generally won't serve it under that name. Apart from the name, it's built for speed. You swallow roughly one to one and a half standard drinks in a few seconds, and people often do several. Fast, large doses like this cause the sharpest jumps in blood alcohol and the highest risk of blacking out. If there's one drink to skip on St. Patrick's Day, it's this one.

### How many standard drinks are you actually having?

In the US, a standard drink contains about 14 grams (0.6 ounces) of pure alcohol. Here's how common St. Patrick's Day drinks compare. These are approximate, because pours and strengths vary.

| Drink | Typical size and strength | Approximate standard drinks |
|---|---|---|
| Light lager or green beer, US pint | 16 oz at about 4 to 5% | 1.1 to 1.3 |
| Guinness Draught, US pint | 16 oz at about 4.2% | about 1.1 |
| Guinness Draught, imperial pint | 20 oz at about 4.2% | about 1.4 |
| Craft IPA, US pint | 16 oz at about 7% | about 1.9 |
| Irish whiskey shot | 1.5 oz at 40% | 1 |
| Irish coffee | 1.5 oz whiskey plus coffee | about 1 |
| Dropped-shot drink | half pint of stout plus about 1 oz of whiskey and Irish cream | about 1 to 1.5 |

A day of eight pints of stout plus two rounds of whiskey shots is roughly 11 to 13 standard drinks. That's a lot more than most people would guess if you asked them how many drinks they had.

## Is "Beer Before Liquor" Real?

The old rhyme says "beer before liquor, never been sicker." A 2019 randomized trial published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* tested this directly by having volunteers drink beer then wine, wine then beer, or just one of the two. The order made no meaningful difference to how bad the hangover was. What mattered was how drunk people got and whether they vomited. So on St. Patrick's Day, switching from pints to whiskey isn't dangerous because of the order. It's risky because it usually means drinking faster. Our article on the [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) covers the research.

## A St. Patrick's Day Game Plan That Still Lets You Have Fun

### The night before and the morning of

- **Get a decent night's sleep on March 16.** Starting the day tired makes everything worse.
- **Eat a real breakfast.** Eggs, toast, potatoes, oatmeal, or a full breakfast with protein and some fat. Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream. The "kegs and eggs" tradition gets the eggs part right. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) has more ideas, and eggs come up again in our [eggs for hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) article.
- **Drink a big glass of water before you go.** Starting hydrated helps.
- **Charge your phone and set up your ride.** You'll thank yourself at 10 p.m.

### During the day

- **Pace yourself at roughly one standard drink per hour.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average, though this varies a lot between people. Faster than that, and alcohol builds up in your blood. Remember that a big pint is more than one drink.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between each round is the easiest habit to keep, and it slows your drinking without you noticing.
- **Eat every few hours.** Plan for lunch and dinner, not just snacks. Pub food like stew, shepherd's pie, or fish and chips is a good excuse.
- **Pick lower-strength drinks.** A session lager or a stout like Guinness carries less alcohol per pint than an IPA. Non-alcoholic beers have improved a lot and are a good way to stay in the round without adding alcohol.
- **Say no to shots and chugged drinks.** These are where the day usually goes off the rails.
- **Keep an eye on your friends.** Agree to check on each other, and don't let anyone wander off alone.

### Before bed

- **Drink water.** A glass or two before sleep and a glass by the bed. Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. That's why you pee so much while drinking and wake up thirsty.
- **Have a snack if you can.** Something with carbohydrates can help with the low blood sugar that adds to morning shakiness and fatigue.
- **Don't take acetaminophen (Tylenol) "just in case."** Taking it before bed while your liver is still busy with alcohol, often on an empty stomach, is a bad idea. If you wake up with a headache, deal with it then.
- **Don't take sleep aids with alcohol.** Products like NyQuil or "PM" pain relievers contain sedating antihistamines that stack with alcohol.

## Hydration and Electrolytes: Do They Help?

Dehydration is part of the hangover picture, though not the whole story. Studies that measure people's hydration don't find a tight link between how dehydrated someone is and how bad their hangover feels, so water alone won't cure it. Still, thirst, dry mouth, and dizziness when you stand up all improve when you rehydrate, and a long day of drinking, sometimes outside, leaves most people short on fluids.

Plain water is fine for most people. An oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix makes the most sense if you've been sweating a lot, vomiting, or had diarrhea, since those lose salts as well as water. For the details on timing, see [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking), and for a head-to-head of popular options, see [Pedialyte vs. Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover).

## The Morning After: Getting Through March 18

If you wake up rough, here's what actually helps:

1. **Rehydrate slowly.** Sip water or an electrolyte drink. If your stomach is upset, small sips every few minutes work better than big gulps.
2. **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, or broth-based soup. Food helps with low blood sugar and gives your stomach something besides acid.
3. **Use a pain reliever carefully, if you need one.** Ibuprofen with food is a common choice for a hangover headache, but it can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already upset. Our guide on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains the trade-offs. Go easy on acetaminophen after a very heavy day of drinking, and never go over the label dose.
4. **Rest.** Sleep is a big part of recovery. If you can push back your morning plans, do it.
5. **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Another drink may delay the worst of the hangover for a few hours, but it adds more alcohol for your body to deal with and pushes the recovery back.
6. **Coffee is fine in moderation.** It can help with grogginess and with caffeine-withdrawal headaches if you're a regular coffee drinker. It doesn't sober you up.

Most hangovers fade within about 24 hours. If you want a sense of the timeline, our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) walks through it. Our list of [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) covers what's worth reaching for.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most St. Patrick's Day hangovers are miserable but harmless and pass within a day. **Get medical care if:** you can't keep any fluids down for many hours or are vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds; you have severe belly pain, chest pain, or trouble breathing; you feel confused, very drowsy, or faint; your symptoms are getting worse instead of better after 24 hours; or you hit your head while drinking and now have a bad headache, repeated vomiting, or confusion. If you drank heavily for several days in a row (a long festival weekend, for example) and then develop shaking hands, sweating, a racing heart, strong anxiety, seeing or hearing things that aren't there, or a seizure, that can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover. Withdrawal can be dangerous and needs medical care, so see a doctor or go to urgent care. Our article on [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains the difference.

## Common St. Patrick's Day Hangover Myths

- **"A greasy breakfast the morning after soaks up the alcohol."** By morning, the alcohol is mostly gone or already in your blood. Food the morning after helps with blood sugar and comfort, but the real benefit of food comes before and during drinking.
- **"Guinness is a meal in a glass, so you don't need to eat."** Guinness has about as many calories as many light-to-regular beers and very little protein or fat. It won't slow absorption the way a real meal will.
- **"Green beer stains your insides."** Food coloring can tint your stool briefly. It doesn't harm your gut.
- **"Switching to whiskey later is what makes you sick."** As covered above, the order isn't the problem. Speed and total amount are.
- **"You can sober up with coffee or a cold shower."** Only time clears alcohol. Coffee makes you a more alert drunk person, not a less drunk one.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people add a supplement to their St. Patrick's Day routine. The most talked-about one is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Here's an honest view:

- **The research is early.** Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies on how DHM affects alcohol metabolism and the liver. Human data are limited, and there's no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people the way some marketing suggests.
- **It doesn't change your blood alcohol level in any way you can count on.** It won't make you safe to drive, and it isn't a reason to drink more.
- **It's not a replacement for the basics.** Food, pacing, water, and sleep do far more for how you'll feel on March 18 than any capsule.

If you want to try DHM alongside those habits, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first. For a wider set of tips that apply to any big drinking holiday, see our [holiday drinking survival guide](/never-hungover/holiday-drinking-survival-guide-health-first-approach) and [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- St. Patrick's Day hangovers are mostly about **how much you drink over a very long day**, not about green beer or day drinking itself.
- **Pints are more than one drink.** A US pint of regular beer is about 1.3 standard drinks, and an imperial pint even more.
- **Eat a real breakfast, eat lunch, and eat dinner.** Alternate drinks with water and aim for about one standard drink per hour.
- **Skip shots and chugged dropped-shot drinks**, which cause the fastest rise in blood alcohol.
- **Plan your ride home before your first drink**, and remember you may still be impaired the next morning.
- **Know the signs of alcohol poisoning**, and call 911 if someone can't be woken up, is breathing slowly, or has a seizure.

**Related reading:** [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking), [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas), [New Year's hangover plan](/never-hungover/new-years-hangover).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why are St. Patrick's Day hangovers so bad?**

Mostly because of how long the day is. Many people start drinking in the late morning and keep going until late at night, often with little real food, large pints that count as more than one drink each, rounds of shots, and a short night of sleep. The total amount of alcohol ends up much higher than on a normal night out, and that's the biggest driver of how bad a hangover feels.

**Does green beer give you a worse hangover?**

There's no good evidence that it does. Green beer is usually a regular light lager with a few drops of food coloring, and the dye isn't known to cause hangover symptoms. The issue is that cheap green beer is easy to drink fast and in large amounts. The food coloring can turn your stool green for a day or two, which is harmless.

**Is day drinking worse for a hangover?**

Drink for drink, there's no good evidence that alcohol in daylight causes a worse hangover than alcohol at night. Day drinking tends to cause worse hangovers because it usually means more hours of drinking, skipped meals, less water, and a disrupted sleep schedule. Starting later, eating lunch, taking a mid-afternoon break, and setting an end time all help.

**How many drinks is a pint of Guinness?**

Guinness Draught is around 4.2% alcohol. A 16-ounce US pint works out to roughly 1.1 standard drinks, and a 20-ounce imperial pint is about 1.4. That's similar to or a little less than a pint of regular lager, and less than a pint of most craft IPAs. Its dark color doesn't mean it's stronger.

**What should I eat before St. Patrick's Day drinking?**

A real breakfast with protein, some fat, and carbohydrates, such as eggs with toast and potatoes, or oatmeal with nuts. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol enters your bloodstream. Then plan to eat lunch and dinner, too, rather than relying on bar snacks. Eating the morning after helps you feel better, but eating before and during drinking does more.

**How do I get rid of a St. Patrick's Day hangover fast?**

There's no instant cure. The things that help most are sipping water or an electrolyte drink, eating something gentle like toast, eggs, or soup, resting, and taking ibuprofen with food if you need a pain reliever. Avoid more alcohol, since a "hair of the dog" only delays recovery. Most hangovers clear within about 24 hours.

**Is it safe to drive the morning after St. Patrick's Day?**

Not always. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average, so if you drank heavily until late at night, you may still have alcohol in your blood the next morning, sometimes enough to be impaired or over the legal limit. If you had a big night, give yourself plenty of time or arrange another way to get where you're going.

**When should I see a doctor after St. Patrick's Day drinking?**

Call 911 for signs of alcohol poisoning: someone who can't be woken, slow or irregular breathing, a seizure, or cold, bluish skin. See a doctor if you can't keep fluids down, have severe belly or chest pain, are vomiting blood, feel confused, or are getting worse after 24 hours. If you drank heavily for several days in a row and then develop shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or hallucinations, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which needs medical care.

**Does DHM prevent St. Patrick's Day hangovers?**

There's no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people. Most research on it comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. Some people use it as part of their routine, but it doesn't lower your blood alcohol in a way you can rely on and isn't a substitute for eating, pacing your drinks, drinking water, and getting home safely.
